landing.hero: Your first year in the US, with a guide and a few friends.
landing.sub: Understand your letters, keep track of important dates, find help you can trust, and meet people who have been through it.
landing.whyIntro: This affects millions of people, but you rarely hear about it. The harm is quiet: a confusing letter, a missed deadline, a fake “notario.”
landing.stat1: of people in completed immigration court cases had a lawyer in FY2026, the lowest since 2010.
landing.stat2: of people who applied for relief without an attorney succeeded, in a national study of 1.2 million deportation cases.
landing.stat3: Spanish-only households have historically been about five times more likely to be unbanked (FDIC survey data).
landing.statsFooter: Notario fraud is badly underreported because victims fear coming forward. Kids often interpret bills, leases and legal letters for their parents.
landing.pitch: The help exists. People just can't find it, read it, or know which part applies to them.
landing.privacy: Sign in with just an email and password. Your plan, dates and questions stay on your phone. We never keep photos of your documents.

notario.title: Notarios Can't Give Legal Advice
notario.short: Only lawyers and accredited representatives can.
notario.body: Only lawyers and DOJ-accredited representatives can give immigration legal advice. A “notario” cannot. In the US, a notary public can only witness signatures.

guarantee.title: No One Can Guarantee a Green Card
guarantee.body: No one can guarantee a green card or put you on a “special list.” If someone promises a result or asks for money to speed things up, it is a warning sign.

forms.title: USCIS Forms Are Free
forms.body: Official USCIS forms are free to download from uscis.gov. Some applications have a filing fee, but the forms themselves never cost money. Official government websites end in .gov.

checkLawyer.title: How to Check a Lawyer
checkLawyer.short: Look them up with your state bar.
checkLawyer.body: Look up a lawyer with the state bar where they are licensed. In Texas, use the State Bar of Texas “Find a Lawyer” search. For accredited representatives, check the DOJ (EOIR) roster.

tenant.title: Tenant Basics
tenant.short: Evictions must go through a court.
tenant.body: Read your lease and keep a copy. A landlord cannot remove you by changing the locks or taking your things; an eviction has to go through a court. If you get court papers, don't ignore them.

workplace.title: Workplace Basics
workplace.short: Minimum wage and overtime apply to most workers.
workplace.body: Most workers must be paid at least the federal minimum wage and overtime for hours over 40 in a week. The Department of Labor takes wage complaints regardless of immigration status. Keep a record of your hours and pay.

checklist.title: Things to Take Care Of
checklist.notFound: This item isn't on your list.
checklist.stepsFooter: General steps written by the Landed team. They are not legal advice.

i94.title: Get a copy of your I-94
i94.short: Your official arrival record. Check the dates on it.
i94.body: The I-94 is the government's record of when you arrived and how long you may stay. Many offices ask for it, and the date on it matters. You can get it free online.

steps.s1: Go to the official I-94 website. It is free.
steps.s2: Choose “Get Most Recent I-94” and type your name and passport details exactly as they are in your passport.
steps.s3: Check your name, your class of admission, and the “Admit Until” date.
steps.s4: Save or print a copy and keep it with your passport.
steps.s5: If something on it is wrong, a CBP Deferred Inspection office can help correct it.

ssn.title: Get a Social Security number
ssn.short: You need it to work and for many other things.
ssn.body: A Social Security number (SSN) is used for work, taxes, and banks. Not everyone can get one. It depends on your immigration status and work permission. The card and the number are always free.

steps.s1: Find out if you can get a number and which documents you need.
steps.s2: Gather your documents: usually your passport, your immigration document, and proof of your age.
steps.s3: Start your application online or go to a Social Security office near you.
steps.s4: Wait for your card in the mail. Keep it in a safe place, not in your wallet.

address.title: Tell USCIS when you move
address.short: Most people must report a new address within 10 days.
address.body: Most non-citizens must tell USCIS about a new address within 10 days of moving. If you don't, you could miss important letters. It is free.

steps.s1: When you move, write down the date. You usually have 10 days.
steps.s2: Change your address online with USCIS.
steps.s3: If you have a case in immigration court, you must also tell the court, using form EOIR-33.
steps.s4: Save the confirmation page or email.

bank.title: Open a bank account
bank.short: Keep your money safe and avoid check-cashing fees.
bank.body: A bank or credit union account keeps your money safer than cash and helps you build a history in the US. Some banks accept a passport or consular ID.

steps.s1: Compare banks and credit unions. Look at monthly fees and minimum balances.
steps.s2: Bring your ID (passport or consular ID) and your SSN or ITIN if you have one. Ask which documents they accept.
steps.s3: Open the account and ask for a debit card.
steps.s4: Avoid check-cashing stores. Their fees are high.

stateId.title: Get a state ID or driver's license
stateId.short: A local photo ID makes many things easier.
stateId.body: A state ID card or driver's license is accepted almost everywhere. Each state has its own rules about which documents you need.

steps.s1: Find your state's driver's license office.
steps.s2: Check which documents your state accepts.
steps.s3: Make an appointment if your state needs one.
steps.s4: Bring your documents and the fee to your appointment.

links.l1: Find your state's motor vehicle office (USA.gov)
links.l2: Texas driver license and ID (Texas DPS)

itin.title: Get an ITIN if you can't get an SSN
itin.short: A tax number for people who can't get a Social Security number.
itin.body: An ITIN (Individual Taxpayer Identification Number) lets you file taxes if you can't get a Social Security number. It does not give permission to work. Tax information is protected by privacy law, but in 2025 the IRS shared some taxpayers' addresses with ICE. Courts have stopped this for now, and the case is still going on. If you are worried, talk to free legal help before you apply.

steps.s1: Check if you need an ITIN. You only need one if you can't get an SSN.
steps.s3: Send it with your tax return, or get free help from an IRS Certified Acceptance Agent.
steps.s4: Wait for the IRS letter with your number. Keep it safe.

taxes.title: File your taxes
taxes.short: Taxes are usually due in mid-April. Free help is available.
taxes.body: If you earned money in the US, you may need to file a tax return, usually by April 15. Filing on time can also help you get refunds and credits. Free tax help is available.

steps.s1: Collect your tax forms from work, like a W-2 or 1099.
steps.s2: Find free tax help near you (VITA).
steps.s3: File your return by the deadline, usually April 15.
steps.s4: Keep copies of your return and forms.

credit.title: Start building credit
credit.short: Credit helps you rent a home and get loans.
credit.body: Your credit history shows how you pay bills. Landlords and lenders look at it. You can start building it slowly and check your reports for free.

steps.s1: Learn what credit reports and scores are.
steps.s2: Get your free credit reports and check them for mistakes.
steps.s4: Think about a secured credit card, and never pay someone who promises to “fix” your credit.

workPermit.title: Know your work permit dates
workPermit.short: Add the expiration date so you don't miss it.
workPermit.body: A work permit (EAD) has an end date. Some people can ask for a new one before it ends. When and how depends on your category, so check the official page and save the date.

steps.s1: Find the expiration date on your card and add it to your dates.
steps.s2: Read when and how you can ask for a renewal (Form I-765).
steps.s3: If you file online, use a USCIS account.
steps.s4: Keep your receipt notice and check your case status.

wages.title: Know your rights at work
wages.short: Minimum wage and overtime apply to most workers.
wages.body: Most workers must get at least the minimum wage and extra pay for overtime. The Department of Labor takes complaints from workers no matter their immigration status.

steps.s1: Learn the minimum wage in your state.
steps.s2: Write down your hours and keep your pay stubs.
steps.s3: If you are not paid what you are owed, you can file a complaint.

links.l2: File a wage complaint (Department of Labor)

health.title: Find low-cost health care
health.short: Community health centers charge based on your income.
health.body: Community health centers see patients even without insurance and charge based on income. Some immigrants can also get health insurance. Emergency rooms must treat you in an emergency.

steps.s1: Find a community health center near you.
steps.s2: Check which health coverage you may be able to get.
steps.s3: Bring ID and proof of income to your first visit.
steps.s4: In an emergency, go to the emergency room or call 911.

school.title: Enroll your children in school
school.short: All children have the right to public school.
school.body: In the US, all children can go to free public school, whatever their immigration status. Schools cannot ask about immigration status to enroll a child.

steps.s1: Contact your local school district office.
steps.s2: Gather proof of your child's age and proof of where you live.
steps.s3: Fill out the enrollment forms. Ask for help in your language.
steps.s4: Ask about English learner support for your child.

selectiveService.title: Register for Selective Service (men 18–25)
selectiveService.short: Most men ages 18 to 25 living in the US must register.
selectiveService.body: Most men ages 18 through 25 who live in the US, including most immigrants, must register with Selective Service. Registering is free and quick.

steps.s1: Check if you need to register. It is mostly men ages 18 through 25.

legalHelp.title: Find free legal help you can trust
legalHelp.short: Know who can give immigration advice before you need it.
legalHelp.body: Only lawyers and DOJ-accredited representatives can give immigration legal advice. Find a free or low-cost legal aid group near you before you need one.

steps.s1: Search for free or low-cost legal help near you.
steps.s2: Make sure the person is a lawyer or a DOJ-accredited representative.
steps.s3: Ask about the cost before your first meeting.
steps.s4: Bring copies of your documents. Keep the originals.

scams.title: Learn to spot immigration scams
scams.short: Notarios can't give legal advice. Forms are free.
scams.body: Scammers target immigrants. A “notario” cannot give legal advice, nobody can guarantee a green card, and USCIS forms are free to download.

steps.s1: Learn the most common immigration scams.
steps.s2: Download forms only from uscis.gov. They are free.
steps.s3: If someone tries to scam you, report it.

tenant.title: Know your rights as a renter
tenant.short: A landlord must go through court to evict you.
tenant.body: A landlord cannot remove you by changing the locks or taking your things. An eviction has to go through a court. Read your lease and keep a copy.

steps.s1: Read your lease and keep a copy.
steps.s2: Ask for repairs in writing and keep copies.
steps.s3: Learn how the eviction process works.
steps.s4: If you get court papers, don't ignore them. Get free legal help.

links.l1: If your landlord locks you out (TexasLawHelp)
links.l3: Landlord and tenant help (Florida Consumer Services)
links.l5: Landlord and tenant disputes and evictions (Arizona Courts)
links.l7: Tenants' rights guide (New York Attorney General)

travel.title: Before you travel outside the US
travel.short: Leaving can affect a pending case. Ask first.
travel.body: For many immigrants, leaving the US can affect a pending application or the ability to come back. Some people need a travel document before they leave. Whether it is safe depends on your situation.

steps.s1: Before you buy a ticket, learn which travel documents exist.
steps.s2: Read about Advance Parole and Re-entry Permits (Form I-131).
steps.s3: Talk to free legal help about your situation before you travel.
steps.s4: Carry your immigration documents when you travel.

benefits.title: Public benefits and your status
benefits.short: Who can get help depends on status. Ask before you apply.
benefits.body: Some programs help with food, health care and housing. Who can get them depends on immigration status, and in some cases using benefits can matter for a future application. Ask free legal help before you apply.

steps.s1: Learn which government benefit programs exist.
steps.s2: Eligibility depends on your status. Ask free legal help what applies to you.
steps.s3: Children born in the US may qualify even if their parents do not.
steps.s4: Always tell the truth on applications.

court.title: If you have an immigration court date
court.short: Never miss a hearing. Check your case online.
court.body: If you have a case in immigration court, missing a hearing can have serious results. You can check your next hearing date online with your A-number.

steps.s1: Check your next hearing date online.
steps.s2: Add the hearing date to your dates.
steps.s3: If you move, tell the court within 5 days using form EOIR-33.
steps.s4: Find free legal help as early as you can.
steps.s5: Go to every hearing, even if you don't have a lawyer yet.

legalHelpCard.title: Talk to free legal help
legalHelpCard.body: This depends on your immigration status. A free legal aid group can look at your situation.
